primary.name: Rio Tinto — SEC EDGAR 6-K filings index
primary.note: Regulated filing feed, not a corporate IR page. Most stable source in the list — SEC EDGAR also has a real JSON API at data.sec.gov/submissions/CIK0000863064.json if we want to move off HTML scraping later.

primary.name: BHP — Media centre releases (Operational Review index)
primary.note: HTML index page. The Operational Review itself links to a downloadable Excel data book — track the index page for the new release, handle the Excel file as a separate follow-up fetch once flagged, not through the text fingerprint.

primary.name: Fortescue — Results and operational performance index
primary.note: HTML index page listing quarterly production reports with dates and PDF links. Track this page, not the PDF links directly — the fetcher has no PDF text extraction yet.

primary.name: Vale — Production and sales report landing page
primary.note: Vale's report pages follow a predictable slug (vale.com/w/production-and-sales-report-{q}q{yy}), confirmed across 1Q25, 2Q25 and prior years. Track this index/landing page rather than constructing the next slug directly, since CMS slug patterns can break silently without warning.

primary.name: Anglo American — Press releases index (quarterly production reports)
primary.note: Confirmed: Minas-Rio is broken out at quarterly cadence with production, realised price (vs Fastmarkets 65% Fe benchmark) and grade all separately reported from Kumba. PDF filenames follow a predictable pattern (q{n}-{year}-production-report.pdf) but track the index page, not the constructed URL, consistent with Vale and Fortescue.

primary.name: Champion Iron — ASX announcements (Bloom Lake quarterly activities report)
primary.note: ASX company announcements page for Champion Iron (ASX: CIA). Genuinely single-asset (Bloom Lake), so this is the cleanest true mine-level source in the list despite smaller volume.

primary.name: ArcelorMittal — SEC EDGAR 6-K filings index (Liberia mining segment)
primary.note: Gap identified and fixed: mine #6 (ArcelorMittal Liberia, Yekepa/Tokadeh) was in the original candidate sheet but missing from this registry, so the weekly job was silently never checking it. Verified via the Q1 2026 6-K earnings release exhibit (CIK 1243429): the Mining segment table breaks out iron ore production and shipment volumes quarterly, separating ArcelorMittal Liberia from ArcelorMittal Mines Canada (AMMC) in the same table. This is better disclosure than the original candidate sheet assumed (it flagged 'may only appear in annual report, not quarterly' — that was incorrect). Same regulated-filing-feed pattern as Rio Tinto, most stable source type in the registry.

market_context.name: USGS — Mineral Commodity Summaries (iron ore)
market_context.note: Annual cadence only. Use for country-level cross-checks and the China reference-only row, not weekly signal.

market_context.name: World Steel Association — Steel statistics
market_context.note: Monthly crude steel output by country — the demand-side context metric for iron ore, mirrors how the copper dashboard uses ICSG refined balance context.

market_context.name: SGX iron ore 62% Fe futures — price reference (via Investing.com, free aggregator quote)
market_context.note: Platts IODEX itself is paywalled, and SGX's own historical settlement data is Platts/TSI-based underneath, so there is no genuinely free primary feed. This is a free aggregator page showing SGX-listed iron ore futures quotes — lower confidence than a primary exchange source, classify as Tier 2 context only, not a Tier 1 fact source. Revisit if TS Lombard obtains a Platts/S&P Global Commodity Insights subscription.

market_context.name: Australian Office of the Chief Economist — Resources and Energy Quarterly (iron ore outlook)
market_context.note: This is the registered third-party outlook/forecaster for iron ore, equivalent to ICSG's role in the copper registry — publishes genuine supply/demand/price forecasts (2-year short-term each quarter, 5-year medium-term in the March edition), not just historical stats. Free, government-published, quarterly cadence. Caveat: forecasts are framed around Australian export volumes/earnings with global supply/demand as context driving the price outlook, not a pure global balance the way ICSG's copper forecast is — still the closest genuine outlook-forecaster available for iron ore. validate_data.py's outlook-scenario check should accept notes citing "REQ" or "Resources and Energy Quarterly" as the third-party forecaster string, alongside "internal".

market_context.name: IBRAM (Instituto Brasileiro de Mineração) — sector investment and production forecasts
market_context.note: Publishes multi-year iron ore investment and production forecasts for Brazil (e.g. 2026-2030 cycle). Free access. Caveat: IBRAM is Brazil's mining industry association, not a government body — treat as a lower-independence tier than REQ (Australian government) or USGS. Useful as regional context for Vale, Minas-Rio; not a substitute for a government-published outlook. validate_data.py's outlook-scenario check can accept notes citing "IBRAM" for Brazil-specific context, alongside "internal" and "REQ".

market_context.name: Natural Resources Canada — Iron ore facts / Annual Statistics of Mineral Production
market_context.note: No genuine ongoing iron-ore outlook publication exists for Canada comparable to REQ (Australia) or IBRAM (Brazil) — checked bank research (RBC, TD, Deutsche Bank) and found only sporadic, largely paywalled sell-side notes, not a structured free forecast. NRCan is a government body and the best available free source, but this is predominantly historical/statistical (production, trade, exploration spend), with only a thin one-year-ahead forecast component collected as part of its Annual Mineral Production Survey. Flag this gap explicitly rather than overstate what NRCan provides — it is not equivalent in forecasting depth to the Australian or Brazilian sources above.

market_context.name: Mysteel — China iron ore port inventory (weekly)
market_context.note: Weekly imported iron ore stockpile levels across China's 47 major ports. Headline figures are published free in Mysteel's weekly analysis articles even though their full downloadable dataset is subscription-based. Used as the standard industry proxy for seaborne market tightness, since China accounts for roughly 70%+ of global seaborne iron ore imports.

market_context.name: SteelOrbis — China iron ore imports
market_context.note: Stable iron ore market and news index carrying SteelOrbis's monthly reports on China's iron ore import volumes. SteelOrbis reports figures released by China's General Administration of Customs secondhand, so this is a free industry-news source rather than the primary customs data feed; classify as Tier 2 context only.

market_context.name: SteelOrbis — Iron ore Capesize freight rates (Brazil-China and Australia-China)
market_context.note: Same stable iron ore market index as the China-imports entry above; also carries SteelOrbis's periodic reports on Capesize freight rates for both the Tubarão-Qingdao (Brazil) and West Australia-Qingdao (the Baltic Exchange's "C5" route) benchmark lanes. Tier 2, secondhand reporting of freight-market data (shipbrokers SSY/Braemar are the underlying assessors), not a primary exchange feed.

market_context.name: IndexBox/Kallanish — Iron ore freight rates roundups
market_context.note: Periodic roundup articles covering both the Tubarão-Qingdao (Brazil) and West Australia-Qingdao (Australia) Capesize freight rates in the same piece, syndicating Kallanish's freight-market reporting. Free, but secondhand — Tier 2, not a primary shipbroker/exchange feed. Articles are individually dated (e.g. monthly "freight rates in [month]" posts), not a single stable page, so a specific new article must be located manually when this index changes rather than assumed from a fixed URL pattern.
